planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Ribston Pippin is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with two compatible pollinators; Ribston Pippin is a triploid variety whose own pollen is not viable, so it needs two different diploid varieties nearby. Raised in Yorkshire, England around 1707 and one of the two parent varieties of the famous Cox's Orange Pippin, it bears medium, orange-red-flushed, lightly russeted apples with rich, aromatic, sharp-sweet flesh that made it one of the most celebrated English dessert apples of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries before its own offspring largely eclipsed its popularity. As a triploid it produces sterile pollen and needs two other diploid apple varieties planted nearby for reliable cross-pollination, and it can be a somewhat biennial, uneven bearer from year to year. Harvest in mid-fall and store for a few weeks, during which the rich, sharp flavor continues to develop and mellow slightly.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Sturmer Pippin needs a long, warm growing season to ripen and store well, and performs best where autumns stay mild. Bred in Suffolk, England in the early nineteenth century from a Ribston Pippin and Nonpareil cross, it bears firm, greenish-yellow apples with dense, crisp, sharply flavored flesh that ripens very late in the season and keeps exceptionally well, sometimes into late winter or early spring under good storage conditions, making it one of the longest-keeping traditional apples grown. Its late ripening and long storage life made it especially popular in Southern Hemisphere growing regions like Australia and New Zealand, where the extended warm autumn allows the fruit to mature fully; in cooler, shorter-season climates it can struggle to ripen well before frost. Harvest as late in fall as the season allows, letting the fruit hang as long as possible, and store cool for a remarkably long keeping period.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Orleans Reinette is a classic French dessert apple that stores well and develops fuller flavor after a few weeks off the tree. An old French variety documented since the eighteenth century, it bears medium-to-large, golden-orange, russet-dappled apples with dense, rich, nutty-sweet flesh long considered among the finest-flavored dessert apples grown in continental Europe, comparable in reputation to Cox's Orange Pippin in Britain. Its excellent, complex flavor and good keeping qualities have kept it a favorite of European apple connoisseurs and heirloom orchardists for centuries, even as it remains less widely known in North America than its English counterparts. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for several weeks to a couple of months, during which the rich, nutty flavor continues to deepen.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun with a compatible pollinator; Adams Pearmain is a reliable, easy-to-grow classic English russet apple well suited to a home orchard. An old English variety first recorded in the early nineteenth century, it bears medium, elongated, pearmain-shaped apples with a dull red flush over a russeted yellow ground and dense, crisp, nutty-sweet flesh, ripening in mid-fall as a reliable, well-flavored traditional dessert apple. Its consistent, moderate cropping and good disease tolerance compared to some other classic English varieties have made it a dependable choice for a home orchard wanting an easy-to-grow heirloom russet-type apple. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a few weeks to a couple of months for the best rich, nutty dessert flavor.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in well-drained soil in full sun; King of the Pippins is a strong, reliable pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties, though it can bear biennially if not thinned. An old variety of uncertain French or English origin dating to at least the eighteenth century, it bears attractive orange-red-striped apples over a golden ground, with crisp, aromatic, sweet-sharp flesh that made it a widely planted commercial dessert apple across Europe for generations before more modern varieties took over the market. Its strong, abundant bloom makes it a valuable cross-pollinator for many other mid-season apple varieties in a mixed home orchard, though the tree has a tendency toward biennial bearing, alternating heavy and light crop years unless fruit is thinned in a heavy year. Harvest in mid-fall and eat within a couple of months, since it does not keep quite as long as some other classic dessert varieties.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste

planting.note: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site with well-drained soil and a compatible pollinator; D'Arcy Spice needs a warm season to develop its distinctive flavor and can be a shy, unreliable bearer.

directions: Plant bare-root trees while dormant in late winter in a warm, sheltered, full-sun site with well-drained soil and a compatible pollinator; D'Arcy Spice needs a warm season to develop its distinctive flavor and can be a shy, unreliable bearer. A rare old English apple originating in Essex in the late eighteenth century, it bears small, dull green-brown, unassuming-looking russeted apples that belie a uniquely rich, warm, nutmeg-and-spice-like flavor unlike any other apple, prized by heirloom enthusiasts and considered one of the most distinctively flavored traditional English dessert apples. It is a late-ripening, long-keeping variety that develops its best spiced flavor only after a period of storage, but the tree can be an unreliable, biennial bearer and needs a warm, sheltered site to ripen and flavor the fruit well, making it better suited to a favorable microclimate than an exposed site. Harvest in mid-to-late fall and store for a month or more before eating, since the distinctive spiced flavor develops and intensifies in storage.
sources: Slow Food USA — Ark of Taste
